10417-love-life-work-being-a-book-of-opi:
Elbert Hubbard published this book of opinions in 1906, promising good-natured advice on how to find happiness with the least harm to others. Hubbard, founder of the Roycroft arts community, writes in short, aphoristic chapters that mix cheer, scolding, and common sense. The book is a miscellany, not a system.

Chapters treat prayer, time and chance, religious revivals, mental attitude, outsiders, art, progress, sympathy, and work versus waste. Hubbard urges initiative, honesty, and kind action over worry about the future. Readers get a brisk, early self-help book, full of maxims on love, life, and work.
10485-experiments-in-government-and-the-:
Elihu Root published this constitutional study in 1913, on experiments in government and the essentials of the American Constitution. Root, a statesman and lawyer, sees two assaults at work: socialism against individualism, and reform against institutions said to fail the social order. He defends liberty and private property as foundations.

Root shows how America changed since 1787, when slow travel kept states apart, to a time when production and trade ignore state lines. Institutions, he argues, must grow with that new life. Readers get a clear, conservative case for constitutional adaptation without abandoning its core.
12296-camps-and-trails-in-china-a-narrat:
Roy Chapman Andrews published Camps and Trails in China as a narrative of exploration, adventure, and sport in little-known China. Andrews, associate curator of mammals at the American Museum of Natural History, led the museum Asiatic Zoological Expedition of 1916 to 1917.

The book opens with a camp on a snow mountain at twelve thousand feet. It then follows caravans along gorges where sides fall hundreds of feet to green torrents. Those torrents rush toward the sea two thousand five hundred miles away. Andrews describes hunting, mapping, and collecting specimens among peoples and places few Westerners had seen. The narrative mixes science with adventure. It shows early twentieth-century exploration at its most confident and curious.
20363-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-6-jun:
The Continental Monthly for June 1864, volume five, number six, covers literature and art. One essay calls a certain religion the most wonderful thing in history. It starts in an obscure corner of an obscure province, it notes. Its founder dies as a felon among felons on a cross.

Its teachers are peasants fettered by a narrow dialect of an unknown tongue. Yet that faith remade the world, the essay marvels in awe. The Monthly served Union readers with essays amid the Civil War. This issue shows its mix of faith, letters, and wartime thought.
20481-continental-monthly-vol-6-no-1-jul:
The Continental Monthly called itself a magazine devoted to literature and national policy. This is its July 1864 issue, volume 6, number 1. It appeared while the Civil War still raged, and its essays weigh the nation's past and future.

One article describes an American institution as built without any regular plan. It grew, the writer says, by gradual additions and by copying European features, from the Revolution to the present. Even so, it has worked with great vigor and effect. The issue shows Northern readers arguing over what the war was making of their country.
20509-daring-and-suffering-a-history-of-:
William Pittenger's Daring and Suffering tells the true story of the Great Locomotive Chase of 1862. Pittenger was one of the Union soldiers who stole a Confederate train in Georgia. Their roll of honor lists men of the Twenty-first and Thirty-third Ohio Volunteers.

The raiders meant to burn bridges and cut the railroad behind enemy lines. Captured, some were hanged as spies, while others escaped or were exchanged. Pittenger wrote from his own suffering in Confederate prisons. His book became the classic account of the raid, and its men received the first Medals of Honor.
7274-poets-of-the-south-a-series-of-biog:
F. V. N. Painter, professor of modern languages at Roanoke College, presents the poets of the South in biographical and critical studies with typical poems, annotated. His preface argues that these singers form a worthy galaxy of talent, yet remain little read even in the South, which might be expected to take pride in them. An age of prose and practical interests, he says, has drifted readers away from poetry.

Painter answers that drift with lives and poems side by side, so that a reader can meet each poet and judge the verse at once. The studies mix fact with criticism, favouring clear judgment over praise. The book serves as an introduction to a regional tradition too often passed over.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cesare-cantu:
Cesare Cantù was an Italian historian and poet born at Brivio on 8 December 1807 and dying at Milan on 11 March 1895. He first studied theology but left the seminary without finishing, not feeling called to the priesthood. Turning to literature, he taught Italian language and literature, first at Sondrio in 1823, then at Como in 1827, and finally at Milan in 1832.

At Como he wrote the verse tale Algiso. His history of the city and diocese of Como made him better known. His Ragionamenti on seventeenth-century Lombard history expressed liberal views on Austrian policy. They earned him thirteen months' imprisonment, whose miseries he described in the novel Margherita Pusterla. About then he began his greatest work, the Storia universale in 35 volumes, reprinted often and translated into English, German, French, and Spanish.
doe-osti-17134351-south-asia-group-for-e: South Asia energy training got its session one, and this DOE virtual training covers the Engage program. The pages record the first session. The trainees get their materials. Session one was delivered. The program was Engage. The training was virtual.
doe-osti-3001268-let-s-stick-together-in: Corn stover flowability got its moisture study, and this DOE report tests particle size and fractions. The pages detail the findings. The biofuel folks get their data. The material was corn stover. The data were biofuel. The findings were detailed.
doe-osti-3005457-multiple-hypothesis-tra: Transmitter ID got multi-hypothesis tracked, and this DOE text covers opportunistic identification. The pages detail the findings. The signal folks get their method. The tracking was multiple hypothesis. The method was signal. The identification was transmitter. The tracking was hypothesis.
doe-osti-3010913-effects-of-dose-rate-on: LiAlO2 pellets got dose-rated, and this DOE text studies microstructure and deuterium. The pages detail the retention findings. The materials folks get their data. The pellets were gamma-LiAlO2. The data were material. The retention was deuterium. The rate was dose.

The materials folks get their data. The components were 316H. The data were material. The steel was printed. The evaluation was performance.

The engineers get their data. The scale was process. The data were engineer. The twins were digital. The abbreviated were report. The engineers were data.
doe-osti-3673458-multi-component-cavity-: Quantum devices need parts that talk to each other — light to matter, molecule to molecule. Aaron Rury studies multi-component cavity polaritons: light-matter hybrids trapped in mirrored cavities. The work aims at tunable entanglement between molecules and clean conversion of photons to electrons.
love-life-work-being-a-book-of-opinions-:
Love, Life and Work is a book of opinions by Elbert Hubbard, dated 1906. Its subtitle promises good-natured views on reaching happiness with little harm to others. The chapters run from a prayer to essays on time, chance, and mental attitude. Hubbard writes on initiative, sympathy, knowledge, and poise.

He scolds the folly of living always in the future. He urges readers to get out or get in line, and to keep the weekday holy. His style is brisk, plain, and full of country common sense. Hubbard ran the Roycroft shops and spoke to plain working people. These short chapters still read like a friendly talk on living well.
nasa-tm-19630010327-lunar-flight-study-s:
B. J. Lisle of Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this study in April 1963. It is volume six of the Lunar Flight Study Series. The topic is trips between Earth and Moon that stay in one plane. Such flat paths are called coplanar transits in the report.

Lisle's abstract says the work maps the geometry of those transits. It links path behavior to changes in launch conditions, called injection. Start and end traits of each path get close attention. Planners of Moon flights needed such maps to pick safe routes. The study was bookkeeping for Apollo's age: which paths work, and how small errors bend them.
nasa-tm-19670022816-effect-of-wing-pivot:
William P. Henderson and Edward J. Ray, of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, studied a swing-wing design in this investigation. The wing could sweep back and forth on a pivot, and it had an M-shaped planform. The question was where to put the pivot, because pivot position changes how the airplane balances.

Tests ran in Langley's high-speed tunnel, with and without tails and engine packs. Moving the pivot outboard, the results show, made an unstable break in the pitching behavior appear sooner. That break also grew generally more severe. The study gave designers a clearer picture of the trade-offs in pivot placement.
nasa-tm-19690008486-fortran-programs-for:
Harry H. Heyson of Langley Research Center presents Fortran programs for wind tunnel boundary interference in this report. Tunnel walls distort the airflow around a model, and interference factors correct the data. The programs here come from an earlier NASA report, TR R-302, and are printed without comment.

Heyson warns readers to study the earlier report's assumptions before using the code. The method computes interference for arbitrary configurations from calculations for a vanishingly small model. Swapping one subroutine adapts the code to a different tunnel. The underlying theory suits models with large wake deflections, such as V/STOL models. Conventional testing at moderate lift can also use the programs with small changes.
nasa-tm-19710009490-observations-of-acti:
Ronald Greeley of the Ames Research Center studied lava tubes while they were still forming in Hawaii. His report describes fluid basalt flows in the Upper East Rift Zone of Kilauea Volcano. In August 1970, lava poured from a vent near Alae Crater. It crossed the Chain of Craters Road inside Hawaii Volcanoes National Park.

Greeley watched the flows and compared them with older written accounts. From that evidence he reasoned about how lava tubes and channels develop. The tubes formed only in pahoehoe, the smooth, fluid kind of basalt flow. The report gives geologists a rare look at tube building caught in the act, not long after it cooled.
nasa-tm-19710018221-shock-and-vibration-:
Andre J Stromquist and Lawrence Hibben of the Lewis Research Center, with Robert S Foley of Aerojet General, reported these tests in May 1971. Their subject was the turboalternator of the SNAP-8 space power system. The machine joined a mercury vapor turbine to a generator. It had to survive the shaking and shocks of launch.

The unit took shock and vibration loads set by the SNAP-8 specification. Staff at Lewis and Aerojet then took the machine apart. Inspection found wear called galling that had shifted the turbine rotor slightly. Movement of the outer bearing rings was also restricted. Some outside plumbing and instruments had failed. Even so, the unit still operated and held its bearing preload.
nasa-tm-19720013274-engine-investigation:
Robert P Dengler, Frederick C Yeh, James W Gauntner, and Gerald E Fallon of the Lewis Research Center ran this blade test in a real engine. Their report came out in April 1972, as NASA TM X-2526. The test blade was a turbine rotor blade cooled by air. Jets struck its leading edge from inside. Lengthwise passages carried air along the chord. A slotted rear edge let the air escape. Most cooling data then came from still laboratory rigs.

The engine ran with inlet gas heat between two thousand and twenty five hundred degrees Fahrenheit. Gas pressure also spanned a working range. The team presents the measured metal temperatures from those runs. Both average and local heat transfer results are included. Engine truth helped check the cheaper cascade methods.
podcast-dannyjones-Y0KsiUg8UtU:
Writer Jordan Rubin takes Danny Jones inside America's shadow war on clandestine chemistry. Rubin has reported on underground drug labs and the people who run them. The episode covers the hidden front of the drug war, where home chemists and federal agents chase each other.

Rubin explains how secret labs make drugs that laws have not yet named. He describes raids, fires, and the cat-and-mouse game over precursor chemicals. Jones asks who these chemists are and what drives them to risk prison. Curious and wary listeners get a rare look at labs in the dark and busts in the light.
podcast-dannyjones-th0tVVOvltU:
Investigative reporter Sean Naylor joins Danny Jones to discuss covert war. Naylor works with fellow reporter Jack Murphy on the Highside project. Their outlet covers secret units and hidden campaigns.

Naylor warns that the CIA is training a new class of global killers. He bases the claim on years of reporting on special operations. Jones asks how such programs stay hidden from the public. The episode gives a reporter's case, drawn from sources and records, about a shadow war that voters rarely get to debate. The claims are grave, and he states them plainly.
poets-of-the-south-a-series-of-biographi:
F. V. N. Painter, professor of modern languages at Roanoke College, wrote Poets of the South to correct a neglect: the South's singers, he argues, are little read even in the South. His book offers biographical and critical studies with typical poems, annotated, so that readers meet each poet through both a life and a selection. Painter blames an age of prose and practical interests for the drift away from poetic truth.

Five leaders receive chief consideration: Poe, Hayne, Timrod, Lanier, and Ryan, the chorus masters of southern verse, though minor poets and their gems are not forgotten. Painter wrote during a southern literary renaissance, when the region was reading more and reclaiming its older authors. His studies are generous, sometimes defensive, and wholly earnest. An educator's brief for the claim that the South's poets deserve a higher place in American letters than they had been given.
the-ancient-church-its-history-doctrine-:
W. D. Killen, professor of church history and pastoral work for the Presbyterian Church in Ireland, traces the ancient church through its first three hundred years. His title promises four threads: its history, its teaching, its worship, and its frame of rule. The New York edition is dated 1859 in Roman numerals.

In a note at the front, Killen thanks Charles Scribner of New York, the first publisher in the old world or the new to urge him on in the task. Scribner's prompt and kind offers, he says, helped fix plans for the book in Great Britain. Every line of this printing was corrected by Killen himself.
the-white-ladies-of-worcester-a-romance-: Florence L. Barclay, author of The Rosary and The Mistress of Shenstone, published The White Ladies of Worcester as a romance of the twelfth century ghosts. Harry E. Townsend drew its endpapers and ground-plan. The pages present here hold the front matter and a partial contents list, so the romance itself does not appear. Early chapters visit a pilgrim at the gospels and find the Bishop of Sauvenac at the shrine of Saint Cuthberga. Later headings promise a bishop's dream, a noble company, and a mighty host.
